as_told: New College, Oxford, was founded in the late 14th century and has a dining hall with great oak beams. When an entomologist found the beams full of beetles, the College Council did not know where to find oaks that big. The College Forester told them that a grove of oaks had been planted when the College was founded, to replace the hall beams, and that each forester had passed the order down for five hundred years: 'You don't cut them oaks. Them's for the College Hall.'
lesson: A well-run institution plans for its needs centuries ahead, as New College did when it planted oaks at its founding to replace its hall beams.
what_happened: The hall's original roof was a flat tie-beam roof; it was demolished in 1786 and replaced by James Pears with a roof hidden by a plaster ceiling, using pitch pine according to the college archives. In 1865 Sir George Gilbert Scott built the present oak roof as an imitation of the original. The college archives say the oak came from the college woods at Great Horwood, Akeley and Whaddon Chase, where trees had grown for several hundred years, but that those Buckinghamshire woods only came to the college in 1441, after its founding, and that leaving some trees to grow on was normal woodland practice, not a plan for the hall.
false_part: No grove was planted at the founding to replace the hall beams; the oaks used in the 1860s grew in woods the college acquired in 1441 and kept under ordinary woodland management, and the medieval roof had already been replaced with pine in 1786.

lesson_verdict.why: English woods were normally run as coppice with standards, in which oak timber trees were grown on for 80 to 100 years, so big oaks existed through routine stewardship rather than a single plan made centuries ahead. The evidence found does not test whether planning centuries ahead works better.

source.what: Forestry Commission Practice Guide, The Management of Semi-natural Woodlands: 3. Lowland Mixed Broadleaved Woods (1994, reprinted 2003), section 'History and traditional management'
source.quote: Standard oaks were grown for 80–100 years.

Open Library full-text searches for New College with oak, beams, forester, hall and beetle: no telling before 1980.

Web search: found Stewart Brand's retelling (How Buildings Learn, 1994, pp. 130-131), which says he heard it from Bateson in the 1970s and that the college archivist and Clerk of Works 'had no idea' about a new grove. A blog page (beebo.org, 2007) quoting Brand links to the New College archives page that calls the story 'nonsense'. Leads only.

Open Library search for "Them's for the College Hall": earliest hit is The Next Whole Earth Catalog (1980); then Brand 1994 and later books. Searches for "is of rather late foundation" and "Department of Medicine at the University of Hawaii" show the 1980 text opens 'Oak Beams of New College, Oxford / I owe this story to a man who was I think a New College student'. So no telling before 1980 was found, but a metadata search cannot rule one out.
